1.1: What is psychology? What is the field of modern psychology? What is academic psychology?
1.2: Psychology comes from two words: 'psyche,' which means 'soul;' it's an ancient Greek word, and 'logos,' which is 'the rational study of.' So, essentially, what we're doing in psychology is the rational inquiry or study of the soul. And you might say, "Well, really? Are you really sitting there in your lab and trying to weigh souls? You have people before they die. You're like, 'He lost six ounces. That's—.'" No. We're not really studying the soul like that.
1.3: What we're trying to study is kind of the human condition, how we see ourselves, how we perceive the world, how we make sense of the world, how we form relationships with people, how we organize ourselves into groups, how all the machinery works of our visual system, our perceptual system, our cognitorium, if that's even a word. So, we're just trying to figure out the human condition.
1.4: Modern psychology is massive. It's a massive field. I work in a building, and you'll go to the —usually upstairs, they've got somebody working with rodents. They do stuff with rodents because that's where you can get the hoods to vent out the roof. Down in the basement, there's usually a clinical facility where you're doing clinical work because that's where you have enough room for a clinic. And so, everything in between. So, we're dealing with a lot of stuff in psychology.
1.5: The field of psychology has been around about 150 years, and I'll give you more history than you ever want to know. So, it's been around a long time. The roots of modern psychology are primarily coming out of medicine, physiology and philosophy. So, imagine a bunch of physicians who were into philosophy, trying to figure out the mind from looking at the body, and that's kind of what started it. It goes back to that.
1.6: Right now, I imagine today there's probably 100 studies published in psychology. 1.7: Psychology's roots go back to ancient Greek philosophy. And I always like starting at the beginning because if you start at the end, it's just a mess. You start at the beginning, you can see the path. But a lot of our ideas go back to Plato. They go back to Aristotle, some of the ancient Greeks, like Hippocrates or Galen, I guess it's Roman, too, the ancient medical physicians.
1.8: Where I like to think of the root of psychology is Plato's allegory of the cave. I don't know if you're familiar with this, but it's this classic story, an allegory in ancient philosophy. It goes something like this. You imagine a group of guys; they could be women, too, in a cave. They're chained up, so they can only look straight ahead. Everyone's chained up. They can only look one direction, and what they see on the wall are shadows from puppets that are behind them or from machines that are behind them, but they see on the wall are shadows.
1.9: And so what they do, when all they're doing is staring at shadows, is they build a whole story of the world of shadows. They go, "This is how the shadows work. This is what they do. This is the story. This is how these things make sense." So, imagine you're in this cave and you're looking at shadows. You're like, "This is the world. Everything's cool."
1.10: And one day you turn around. You break your chain out, and you look around, and you're like, "Wait a second. This is weird." And you turn around, and you go, "Oh, my God. There's all these machines back here, these giant metal puppets. They are not shadows. The world isn't shadows; it's metal puppets." And behind that puppet's a guy with a big fire. "That's weird. I can barely see the fire." And you crawl out, and you go, "Man, the world isn't what I thought. It's a world of machines and fires."
1.11: And then—this is Plato's story, so it just keeps going—Plato says, "Imagine you get to the fire, and you look up, and you go, 'Oh, my goodness, there's something outside the cave.' You start crawling out of the cave, and you get up there, and it's so bright you can't even see. You look at the grass, and you start to see the grass. You go, 'Whoa! Grass! This is amazing! I can't believe it!' And you stay up on the earth for a little while, and your eyes adjust, and pretty soon you can actually see the sun, and you go, 'Whoa! I didn't imagine anything like this was possible, living in my little shadow cave with all my shadow cave buddies.'"
1.12: So then, Plato says, "Now, go back to your buddies in the cave." So, you crawl back in the cave. You get back, they chain you back up. You're looking at the shadow puppets again. What do you think? Well, you think they're shadow puppets. You don't think it's the same thing. It's not the world you thought it was. You go, "Oh, what I thought was the world is just a pale illusion. What I see is just a thin, narrow illusion of reality. That's weird."
1.13: So, you go to tell your buddies, you're like, "God, you guys don't know, but what we're seeing is just shadows, and there's really a sun out there, and I can't even describe it to you because it's so massive and big, you wouldn't even believe it." And you tell your friends that, and they look at you and go, "You're a freaking lunatic. We're going to put you to death to help us relax." Sort of Plato's story, or Socrates' story.
1.14: So, what this story captures is so much about psychology. First is, what we perceive in the world is not really what's in the world. What we're working on is a model of the world. The other thing that it really captures is how social our psychology is. We're talking about the study of the soul, but we're social animals. This is what Aristotle said, "Humans are social animals." And so, even if we see what's truth, if it doesn't align with everybody else, it's going to lead to social problems. So, there's a very social component for reality.
1.15: It also suggests that there's a way to grow. So, it captures this idea of human development, this idea that you can have one set of views when you're at a certain age, but you can grow beyond that to see something bigger, to have some adventure, to have a journey. It's really an early version of the hero's journey and return back to people.
1.16: So, anyway, I love that story, but it really captures so much of what we're going to talk about in this course, which are these important aspects of the human condition. Anyway, that's Plato's cave. Great starting spot, but there's more in old psych.
1.17: Another great allegory was Plato's allegory of the chariot, and this became the basis of a lot of modern motivational thoughts. So, Plato said, "Imagine you're a chariot driver going through your life, and you have two horses. And one of those horses is noble, and it's working towards the highest aspects of the human condition. It's wonderful. And your other horse is slovenly and tired in a little bit of a sloth, and it's your bad horse. And that's like life, that you're trying to navigate through life with these two different horses that are pulling different ways.
1.18: That model of our motivation and the conflict in the human motivation, which might be the shadow and the ego in a Jungian system, or it might be the ego and the id in a Freudian system, but that idea that we're pulled in different directions is really important for psychology. Human life is complicated. We're always in some conflict. That's our nature. That's why the Buddhists said life is suffering. It's just we're built kind of weird. So, that's another great one.
1.19: A few other things I wanted to point out from the ancient world. One is this great insight by the Greek Heraclitus: "You can't step in the same river twice." You look at the fragments; it's basic, but people always say, "It's not the same river. It's not the same person." So, there's this idea that even though we see the world as stable, our world and even our self is always changing. It's the same river, but the material is always changing. So, when we think about something like, 'Who are we?' When we talk about the self in this class, the self is something that changes all the time. It's dynamic. It's like a river. It's not something stable.
1.20: A lot of our modern clinical psychology has its roots in Greece and Rome. So back then, they talked about things like the humors, like maybe black bile that led to something like depression. So, there's a lot of old medical work back then where they're trying to deal with mental illness, looking at the human condition. T he models were older: earth, wind, fire, and water. The stuff we use now is a little more complicated, but the roots are the same. So anyway, that gives you some idea that these ideas have been around a long time.
1.21: In the West, when the Renaissance came around—Middle Ages, you start getting the Renaissance thought and people start asking these questions again. They start asking questions about psychology, again, from more of a philosophical perspective.
1.22: One of the famous thinkers that influenced how we think about the world is Descartes. So, you've probably heard this Descartes classic cogito, "I think, therefore I am." So, Descartes was trying to figure out, "How do I know I'm a person? How do I know there's not some demon that's convinced me I'm real, but I'm really not real?" And what he concluded in his meditation was that the idea of reflexive thinking, the idea that I can reflect and see myself as a person, gives me confidence that I'm a person. It's a little bit circular. So, Descartes really set up a model of mind that we have in the West as something separate. We call it the mind-body split or mind-body dualism.
1.23: It's probably wrong in a way, but this idea has permeated psychology a great deal. We think of ourselves as our mind is separate from our body, though, in psychology, we're better at that. We also think humans are different than dogs, thanks to Descartes. Humans have superminds, and dogs have just little minds. We have souls. I don't really think that's the case, but that comes out of Descartes.
1.24: So, there's lots of great philosophy in the Renaissance, a lot of interest in how the mind works. 1.27: I want to talk about four key figures that set the tone for what psychology is. I'll talk about the 1800s; then I'm going to go to the 20th century and bring you up to date, so you don't fall asleep yet.
1.28: So, in modern psychology, probably the foremost figure, if you ask people who really started this ball rolling, he's not my favorite guy, but he probably gets the credit for it, is Wilhelm Wundt. So, Wundt was this now famous German—I guess we call him a psychologist, physiologist. He was training in physiology. And what Wundt was doing was trying to figure out the structure of the mind in very basic ways.
1.29: For example, having people memorize things and watching how memory decayed over time. So, if I remembered—like, I came in here today and I remembered everybody's name, and you could have just checked me every minute, and you'd watch those names just slowly disappear from my mind till at the end, I'm like, "Hey, bro." So, that's memory decay. So he was interested in things like that.
1.30: There was another thing, and this goes back to a researcher named Fechner, who's a pre- psychologist, something called a 'just noticeable difference.' This sounds really trivial, but it's important. So, imagine you're holding two weights, and the psychologists say, "Is one heavier than the other?" If they're close, if it's like an ounce and a mini ounce, whatever is smaller than an ounce, an ounce and a gram, maybe I can't tell the difference. But if it's an ounce and an ounce and a half, maybe I can tell the difference. And you can start raising weights and looking at what's called this just noticeable difference. And what Fechner realized was there's actually some math behind it; there's some physics behind that; there's a certain formula or an algorithm that allows you to tell those differences.
1.31: Well, you might go, "What does that have to do with psychology? That's just perception." But that same model, 50 years later, people applied to attitudes, "Hey, maybe we can measure attitudes the same way. So that's where—and I'll talk about that in a second. I'm jumping ahead. So, a lot of these really basic physiological findings translated into more complex, psychological findings later on.
1.32: So, Wundt was working with Fechner and Helmholtz, started this first psychology lab, started training a lot of people in what we call the psychology of functionalism; like I said, it's how to break down the mind, almost like chemistry, into parts and how they work together. It's very important.
1.33: In the US, we had a little different tradition. The US psychology was founded by a gentleman named William James. He was a genius. I guess every one of these people are geniuses. 1.34: James was interested in all sorts of things, but his approach, rather than being structural, was much more about function. James did—he did really interesting work. He was out there. 1.36: James got very into a religious experience. He was experimenting with psychedelics back in, 100 years ago before anybody else. He was using nitrous oxide, which was very big at the time. 1.37: What else did William James—another thing just getting at this early physiology—James was in his lab. He was interested in what's called the reflex arc. So, what they found out was you could take a frog leg, a dead frog. You just take a leg, hook it up, and then shock it with electricity, and it would click together like that. People were shocked, but really, we can just animate life with electricity. James goes, "Oh, my goodness, look. A frog works like this." He developed a model of habit. So, when we talk about building habits, William James built his idea of habits from the reflex arc in frog legs.
1.38: What James said was, "If you work on something and develop these little patterns of behavior, you'll build them up over time, like chains. And if you do the hard work when it's easy—" So, James would say, "Every day, do something hard, that's challenging, because some days you're going to have to do something that's hard and you're going to be able to do it." So, this idea of habit comes out of, essentially, the action of frog legs under electricity.
1.39: So, there's a real emergence of modern psychology. L ooking at big things out of basic physiology is very direct, and we just don't think about it so much because it's been about 100 years. So, James is a huge figure, I'd say a father of functionalism and psychology. So, we have structuralism and functionalism.

1.46: And the fourth person that's really important in the birth of psychology was Ivan Pavlov, who's famous for Pavlov's dog. So, Pavlov was a Russian physiologist. He was working on learning in animals. And what he found was—what he developed was associationist learning. We often call it classical conditioning. So, here's how it works. You find in nature a natural stimulus and response that just exists in nature.
1.47: So, for example, you have a dog, I've got Killarney and Murphy, and I come home, and I open up a bag of cookies, and the first thing that happens is Murphy jumps up on a chair and starts to salivate, literally drool. He's learned to associate that or pair that with me opening a bag of cookies. So, he hears the cookies and starts to salivate. That's associationist learning. That's classical conditioning. It's classical. It's not based on reward. It's based on association. Operant conditioning the Skinnerians based on reward; this is based on association.

1.53: So, what are the forces? Well, the first big force in 20th-century psychology was behaviorism. This is done by a guy named John Watson and later B. F. Skinner, who probably people are familiar with. That's who they named the principal after on the Simpsons, Principal Skinner. What the early learning theorists were really interested in was a kind of conditioning. Instead of classical conditioning, we call it operant conditioning. What it was doing was using strategic rewards and punishments to shape behavior.
1.54: The classic way of doing this in Skinner's world was to take something like a pigeon or maybe a rat, put it in a box called a Skinner box, you'd have a light that went on and off, they would have a thing they could peck and get a food pellet, and they would learn certain things. So, they might learn, "Oh, a combination of lights. If you peck, you get a food pellet." And then, they change the reinforcement. So, this is all about reinforcement schedules. So, do you get a food pellet every time you peck? Do you get a food pellet every three times? Do you get a food pellet on average every three times? Which is called variable ratio reinforcement. How does that make a difference?

And so Kurt Lewin was trying to use very simple social models to understand things like democracy.
1.62: So, in one of his famous studies, he had three groups; I think they were Boy Scouts doing projects. And he said, "Okay, you guys be the democratic team, and you be the authoritarian team, and you be the laissez-faire team." So, the laissez-faire team—the leader's like, "Do whatever you want, guys. Laissez faire capitalism." And then, in the authoritarian team, the leader's like a little Hitler, and he's like, "Do this, do this. Here are the rules." And then, the democratic was, "Hey, you guys will vote and figure out what to do, and then we'll work together." Kurt Lewin found that they had a better time and were more productive in a democratic little system, and he was very happy about that because he'd immigrated to America and a democracy. So, this is the birth of a lot of group behavior, and small group behavior, and social psychology, which is still going on.
1.63: After World War II, you get some other interesting stuff as well. Abraham Maslow, and we'll talk about this when we talk about motivation theory, started in the 1940s in Brooklyn, New York, trying to figure out human motivation. He wrote a very famous paper on how motivation works and human needs. This started the school known as humanism. Think of Carl Rogers is another person of this. There's some older roots in California, out in the Echelon Institute, like Fritz Perls.
1.64: But what happened was there was this big interest in the '40s and '50s in understanding human growth and understanding the human experience. It was after the war. We're getting a little more selfish. We have a little more wealth in our nation. And people got into them—they got into themselves, and this is what turned into the '60s: this human potential movement, the human growth movement, all that came out of 1940s psychology, especially Maslow.
1.65: And then, we had a couple of big, other big changes. There was the cognitive revolution that happened in psychology in the 1960s. What kicked that off was the computer. We didn't really have computers. We couldn't really do it when computers took over in the '60s, '70s, '80s, everybody got personal computers. I think I was, I got my first computer— it must have been like '82 or something. Before that, people had typewriters. Some of you remember; I'm guessing most of you don't.
1.66: When people started getting computers, they thought, "Oh my goodness, the mind must be like a computer. The human mind must work like a computer." This is what we do. Whenever we have new tech, we're like, "The mind must be like this." So, in Freud's day, it was like, "The mind must work like a steam engine." And Aristotle was like, "The mind must work like a leaky bucket." And now we're like, "T he mind must work like AI." No, no, the mind's a different deal, but this is just what we do as humans. So, we had this computer revolution, this big interest in cognitive psychology and how the mind worked, how memory worked, how decisions worked, how judgments worked. The stuff I'll talk about today is a lot of that 80s cognitive social psychology. So, that made a huge difference.
1.67: And then finally, the last, and I think the biggest, and it's what the big push has been now is in the 1990s, we developed technology to image the brain. So, we call this neuroimaging. In 1970, if I wanted to see how behavior affected the brain, what I would do is take some rats, I'd have them do the behavior I was interested in, I'd kill them—I'd sacrifice them, as they call it—and then I'd slice their brain up and put their diet under a microscope and see it. That's how we would see what's going on in the brain. So, you have them do it, kill them right in the middle of it, chop their brain up, and look at a microscope. That works great. The only problem is you're slaughtering rodents and you can't do that with humans. I mean, who knows nowadays? But ethically, we can't do that.
1.68: So, we couldn't look at the human brain, but then we developed neuroimaging, something like a functional MRI, an MEG, an EEG, different things so y ou can measure the brain. And what we were able to do was put people in the scanners and have them do stuff. So, you can be in a scanner and watch a screen. Or you get rejected, "Oh, Keith, you're rejected. How do you feel?" "Oh, I don't know." "Let's watch your brain." So, you put people in a scanner. It's not perfect. It's not as good as chopping up the brain and magnifying it, but you can have people live through this.
1.69: And so, the '90s became, I think it was George Bush senior who declared it 'the decade of the brain,' and they just started pumping money into it. So, we've been pumping money into neuro research for 30 years now. I don't know how far it's gotten, but we have pretty good maps of the brain, we have really good maps of the mouse brain now, and this stuff is, I don't know, it's going to turn into something. But I think neuroscience is probably the hottest stuff we have right now, except for the AI working in with that, which is—anyway, I'll stop. It could be really interesting.
1.70: So, what does psychology look like now? It's like I said: it's big. It is just a big field. I'm a professor. I can go talk to another professor and not have a clue what they're doing. And the way I learn stuff is I might hang out with somebody and go, "Well, how does that work?" And they'll just sit down, have a cup of coffee, and they'll tell me about it. It's just hard to keep up with everything.
1.71: But one way I think it's really useful to think about the field is that we start off as the study of the soul, but really, we're studying all these different levels of analysis. So, I can—let's say I'm interested in something like depression. That's a normal psychological construct; people kind of know what it is. Well, I could study depression at different levels.
1.72: I can look at the role of molecules in depression: "What molecule do I take to make me less depressed? What? Is it serotonin? Is it something else?" I can look at genetics. I can say, "Hey, does depression go in families? If so, what made it go in families?" So, I can do what they call behavioral genetics of depression. I can look at the level of the brain. I can look at the brain circuit: "Oh, is it the old model of depression? Oh, you're missing serotonin." This was never a good model, but I think people know it's not a good model now. I can look at the synapses, or I can look at the structure of the brain, how parts of the brain are talking to other parts of the brain, or I can look at the whole structure of the brain. I can look at the white matter, the gray matter. I can do all sorts of stuff; I can do a lot of stuff just at the level of the brain.
1.73: I can go beyond that and look at the physiological system. I can look at the vagus nerve, I can look at blood pressure, I can look at pulse rate. I can use what we call physiological measures. Those used to be really hard to get. Now I can just wear an Apple watch and get them all. I used to need a whole lab to measure these things.
1.74: I can look at thinking processes: "How are you thinking if you're depressed? Do you see the world as positive? Or maybe you put a little negative spin on things? Maybe your prediction of the future is a little more negative than it should be. Maybe more positive." I can look at the level of attitudes or values: " Do you have attitudes that are making you a little depressed? Maybe you have a little bit of pessimism about the world, and maybe that's feeding into your depression.
1.75: I can look at the level of the self: "So, why are you depressed? Why don't I have a positive attitude about myself? I don't like myself that much. That's part of it. Maybe it's my personality. Maybe I'm a little neurotic. Maybe I tend really well to risks in the environment, and that's translated into my depression."
1.76: I can look at the level of the couple or the relationship: "What's going on in your life that makes you depressed? Are you having struggles with your spouse? Are you having struggles with your friends or the problems at work? Is there something social that's caused it? Maybe what you need are new friends. Maybe your brain's fine, your molecules are fine, your genetics are fine, everything's great; you just need a better friend because your friend sucks. So, that could be a problem.
1.77: I can look at the small group because all these things are different. I can say, "Maybe your workplace is just bringing you down," and people like that. "I'm in a toxic workplace. I got rid of that, and I felt better."
1.78: I can look at the culture you're in. I can say, "Is this a healthy culture? Is this a culture that supports health, that supports sleep, that supports love, that supports people having opportunity? Or is this a culture that makes people not sleep and be stressed and feel doomed all the time? That's going to make you more depressed."
1.79: I can look at your nation-state. I can look at your broader environment. So, there's a whole field of environmental psychology. When we talk about seasonal affective disorder, that's essentially an environmental model of depression. When I don't get enough sun, it's the winter season, my depression goes up. So, the cure for that is you get a light box at home, like a little sun, and you stand by that sun a few hours a day, and that cures it.
1.80: And I can go something even higher, maybe talk about the spiritual level, the collective unconscious. I can go all crazy Carl Jung on you, and I don't know how to do that. But maybe there's something going on bigger than that.
1.81: My point is that when we talk about modern psychology now, we're dealing with things at very, very different levels of analysis, and they all work a little different. And so, you can have one person really interested in the neuroscience of depression or the neuroscience of happiness—I'll make it more happy in here. It's bringing it down—the neuroscience of happiness. And I can have another person, an organizational psychologist, that I want to make a happy workplace. So, they're both interested in happiness and psychology, but just on a different level. Does that make sense?
1.82: So, there's just a lot going on with levels, and it gets really confusing because we change at every one of these levels. We're just different things at every level. So, that's what's going on with psychology. It's just massive, and we're studying things at lots of different levels. You can study anything you want in psychology, pretty much. You don't even have to study people. There's wonderful work on rodents, but there's also wonderful work on other primates: great work on chimpanzees, for example. So there's lots you can do.
1.83: I think what holds psychology together, what makes it psychology and not something else, is the scientific method. It's that we're all trained to do science. Well, what does that mean? It doesn't mean I 'm the science. It means there's a certain way we go about defining problems, defining what we're studying, and then looking at how we're studying.
1.84: The first thing we do in science is we spend a lot of time defining the variables we're looking at. So, if I'm interested in something like happiness, I literally have to define what that is. If I'm interested in depression, I have to define it. And I'm not going to go into that because it's a lot of work. But usually, what that means is reading the history, reading the philosophy, spending some real time thinking like, "What the heck is happiness? What the heck is depression? What the heck is psychic energy? What are these things we're talking about?"
1.85: Once I define it, I have to be able to measure it. I have to be able to assess it. So, I have to build a scale to measure it. If I'm going to do research on depression, I need a depression scale, and we have a lot of good ones: the Beck Depression Inventory, the California Epidemiological Survey of Depression, for example, we have varieties of these, Hamilton. So, we need to develop good assessments, and we need to develop good, what they call operationalizations: I need to make this in the lab.
1.86: So, one thing I got interested in my own research was ego threat, which is how people respond when you hear bad, negative things. "What the heck is ego threat?" Well, when you hear something that's negative about yourself, that's threatening to how you see yourself. "How do you do that in a lab? How do you make people feel that?" Well, it's hard to do, but one way you do it is that you say, "Hey, we're going to do a test on something really important, a nd by the way, you just failed. Damn you!" That's an ego threat. That's how you operationalize it. So, we spend a lot of time thinking about these things.
1.87: If somebody starts talking to me about something, I go, "How do you measure that? How do you measure a change?" And they go, "I can't." Well, I'm like, "Well, dude, you're just doing word salad. That's cool. You can do your talk talk stuff, I don't care, but it's not really useful. It's not science; it's just word stuff." So, when you notice people discussing things, how do you measure it? How would you know if it went up or down? You're talking about all this stuff. How are we going to really get a handle on this? Science. You got to do that. And the science—the part that really makes the science work is spending time thinking about what you're measuring. It's not so much doing the stuff; it's thinking about what you're doing. So, we spend a lot of time assessing things.
1.88: Then, what we do is once we measure these things, we call them constructs, psychological constructs like depression, ego threat, or happiness. I got to get some other examples here that are popular: creativity; that's a good one popping into my head. I have a buddy who studies creativity. We have a lot of discussions about it; it's really complicated.
1.89: Once we figure out how to measure these things, we just start to see how it goes together. So, a lot of times what we do is just associationist work. This correlates with this. People are happy; they spend time outdoors: "Oh, that's interesting. They correlate." So, we do a lot of correlational work.
1.90: And then, if we want to get a little more sophisticated, we try to do experiments. So, instead of just saying, "Hey, it seems like people who are outdoors are happier," I'm going to do an experiment. What I'm going to do is take two groups of people—I'm going to take a group of people, I'm going to randomly assign them just with my number generator: you go in the group that spends time outdoors, and you go in the group that spends time indoors. Then, I'm going to have them spend time outdoors and indoors, and then I'm going to measure their depression. And if I find the outdoor people have less depression than the indoor people, in my experiment I go, "Well, maybe being outdoors is causing a change in depression." So, I'm starting to build a causal model. Does that make sense? So, you go from 'things go together' to 'things cause each other.'
1.91: And then, what we do is we get a little more complicated. We go, "Why did that happen?" So we say, "Yeah, being outdoors made you less depressed. Why is it?" And your neuro guy goes, your buddy in neuro comes up, and she's like, "I think it's the serotonin's release from the"—I don't know anything about this story. "The solar energy goes into your eyes and makes serotonin happen with the magic serotonin maker." That sounds like a pretty good model.
1.92: And somebody else says, your friend that does social sciences, "I bet if you're outside, there are a lot of people walking dogs, and I bet it's just the dogs that make people happy. It's just, it's doodles. It's just doodles." So, they come up with their doodle model. And so, you run your experiments. You say, "Well, is the doodles that did it? Is it the brain magic juice that did it?" And you tease that stuff out. It's research for mechanisms, essentially, for causation. So, that's one thing.
1.93: The other thing we spend a lot of time doing is, when something happens, can you turn it on and off? "Oh, this works like this, but maybe I can turn it off by—maybe the sun will make you less depressed unless I make you read really bad poetry. That will help turn it off." So, I get a bad poetry condition and turn it off. That's what we call moderation. So, essentially, what we're doing is, "Hey, we learn to measure these things. They go together. Here's why they go together. Here's the mechanism, and here's how I can turn it off on and off." That's the moderation, that's science. We're building very, very simple models of a very complicated world.
1.94: So, I sometimes think of my job as—I mean, I'm a personality psychologist. I think of my job as making maps, like a cartographer. I make a map of the world. People are like, "I'm going to go deal with people. Here, take my map of how people work," and they go out and use my map. And it's helpful a little bit, but then they get to certain places where my map isn't helpful, and I'm like, "Well, better get you another map for those places." So, I build another map. So, very much what we're doing is making these very simplified models of the world that we hope are useful, and we hope people use them to make other models.
1.95: What we're not doing is figuring out how the world works perfectly and describing the whole damn thing. We're making simple models, not super complicated models, because we can't do that very well, which is—so, science is very small in a lot of ways. It's very limited what we're doing. So, when people think, when they tell you they're a psychologist and they have stuff figured out, I would always question that. Usually, the more you interact with the world, the less you realize you know. A nyway, so that's pretty much it.
1.96: The other thing to say that can be a problem is never to fall in love with your own models because it's just a darn model. So, you make a model, and what happens is mostly our models are wrong. It takes me about five to seven years to think something through. That sounds crazy, but that's about what it takes. If I have to think something through, it's about five years of my life. If it's hard, five to ten years. You can't just figure stuff out. A dissertation, a PhD is about four or five years of thinking about a topic, and you pretty much handle it. So, this is a really long, slow process, and the world's really complicated. It's not like we got it figured out and can tell everybody.
1.97: In terms of what modern research psychology looks like, we tend to divide it into fields, and they're often by levels of analysis. But it's not really perfect because there's applied psychology, which is the psychology that we use in the world, and then there's more research psychology, which isn't applied, but I'll give you an example.
1.98: So, if you go to any big research university, you're going to have some basic experimental psychology that looks at something like rodents; they might call it behavioral neuroscience or something along those lines, looking at rats. Y ou're going to have some human neuroscience, maybe cognitive neuroscience. This is looking at people, often using scanners like an fMRI. You might have cognitive science or cognitive psychology looking at things like memory, perceptual systems. You're probably going to have a social psychology group doing a lot of things about the self, social relationships, groups, prejudice, lots of these real social issues. You might have personality psychology looking at self.
1.99: And then, in terms of applied fields, what you might have and very likely to have is clinical psychology, which most people are familiar with, which is training people to be clinicians, to go out and work in psychology. Less common, but pretty common still, is industrial psychology. This is people who go into workplace psychology. So, in a department, you'll have people working with rats and people getting dressed up to do corporate work. The same department, just at very different levels of analysis. So, you have all those classic levels.
1.100: Developmental, that's another classic field. So, you have developmental. What's interesting is developmental goes across areas because it's about change, and applied areas are more focused on application. And then, on top of that, you'll have neuroscience attached to everything now. So, you might have cognitive neuroscience, social neuroscience, behavioral neuroscience. You have a lot of interest in neuroscience that's appended to psychology. So, you have all these different levels of analysis and standard fields, each with their own organizations, their groups, their journals, etcetera.
1.101: Another interesting way to break down psychology—and people don't think about it as much in the field, but I think it's useful—is maybe to think about psychology coming from the inside and the outside. So—and this is just how I think of it—outside psychology is this interest in understanding, predicting, and controlling behavior. This is the Skinnerians, "Why are you doing psychology?" "I want to understand behavior so that I can predict behavior, and once I predict behavior, then I can control behavior." So, this is learning psychology is a tool for manipulating people, ideally to make the world better. You don't use these powers for bad, hopefully, but sometimes that happens. But that's how you're thinking about it. It's how I can control or shape people with psychology.
1.102: And then, there's inside psychology, which is the psychology of growth. This is what we're interested in when we read books at the airport and stuff. It's like, "How do I, as a person, start where I am and grow into something more?" Something like humanistic psychology. This is often what you're doing in clinical psychology. It's trying to find out who you are and get better. You're doing this in the workplace with coaching: How do you find somebody who's a leader? And you want to bring a leader into high performance. So, there's an inside psychology about growth, and an outside about control, both different.
1.103: And I wanted to quickly tell you about myself because my own story in psychology, I think, will help make sense a little bit. My story is different than a lot of people, but similar to a lot of people as well. I started—my interest in psychology came from philosophy and psychoanalysis. So, I was just a kid in California, just reading Freud, reading a bunch of Buddhist books, reading Jung, and reading a lot of old philosophy. I didn't understand science at all, and I was a terrible student. I took some good courses at Berkeley, but like I said, I was a terrible student, but I wanted to go into psychoanalysis. I thought that was a thing back then. I ended up meeting a psycho analyst from Arkansas, fishing. He goes, "I'm the last psychoanalyst in Arkansas. I'm an anachronist." He goes, "I was into anachronism the day I got my degree." Well, I guess I'm not going to be a psychoanalyst. They're not many anymore, but that was my interest.
1.104: So, I got a master's degree at San Diego State, home of the fighting Aztecs, with a guy named George Matt, and I spent my time studying mood and memory, the most boring thing you can think of. But it was wonderful to me because that's when I learned how science worked. I learned, essentially, you put people in certain moods, and then you put them in the same mood, and they remember things the same. That's state-dependent memory. So, I got into that, which was a little boring, but I wanted to study the self, a nd I got lucky and had a guy named Constantine Setekides at the University of Wisconsin Madison say, "Come work in my lab. We'll study the self, and we're going to study how people enhance themselves and how people think they're a big deal." So, I got into that work of self-enhancement, and I started studying narcissism, and this is how it worked.
1.105: People are always like, "Why did you study narcissism?" Well, I was at yield waffle shop or yield pancake shop in Madison, Wisconsin, and we were trying to figure out why some people are self-centered sobs when they're with people they love and why other people are pretty nice. And somebody said, "Hey, maybe it's narcissism." I thought, "Well, I'm a closet Freudian. I must be a narcissist. Let's study narcissism." That's how I started doing it. It was just to figure that stuff out because I like Freud. So, a lot of this stuff is just coincidence. I ended up doing it. So, I did that.
1.106: Then, I did a postdoc at Case Western Reserve in Cleveland with a guy named Roy Baumeister, who's a genius in the field of psychology. And my job was on Tuesday nights, I go to his office over Lake Erie, I think. Was that Lake Michigan? I even get the lakes wrong; it's been so long. And his room is all covered with African masks. Oh, the guy was so smart. He still is so smart. And he'd put on acid jazz and he'd go, "Let's talk about big ideas." So, my role was like a sparring partner. We talk about the nature of the world for like five—we'd stay up till two in the morning, then I'd go home and do it again. It was great training. It was so much fun. That was a postdoc. Sorry, you get your PhD, then you spend two years not getting paid, hanging out in Cleveland, and I really got into studying narcissism.
1.107: Then, I ended up at the University of Georgia, where I am now, in Athens. I was at Chapel Hill. Wisconsin, Chapel Hill, Case Western, and I've been at Georgia ever since. My work is mostly on things like narcissism and the self and self-enhancement. So I'm interested in that. I have some weird interests. I'm just talking. I'm interested in shamanic medicine. So, I spend a lot of time studying ayahuasca. I study wealth, so I spent a lot of time studying wealth science. So, I do some other things, too, but it's mostly the ego and the self and those questions.
1.108: I've worked with people that are more sociological. Science is a team sport. And so a lot of my work has been with a colleague named Jean Twenge, who's really interested in sociology. She's a postdoc with me. So, we used to hang out in a basement in Cleveland talking about how the culture worked and talking about generational change and stuff. So I've been really lucky to work with her.
1.109: I've got another colleague, Josh Miller, who's a clinical psychologist, a clinical personality psychologist, who's brilliant. So, I was able to do a lot of clinical work. So, people are like, are you a clinical psychologist? No, I don't talk to people, but I do a lot of work with really talented clinical people.
1.110: So that's what I do. I'm just curious about stuff. The world is far more—I like questions more than answers. And if you ask me how the world was 20 years ago, I see it as much more complicated now than I did 20 years ago. I realize I know nothing. I used to think I was pretty smart. Like 18, I knew everything. Now, I know nothing about the world. It's just awesome.
1.111: Finally, I wanted to wrap up here. I think the time is good. I wanted to say this to people. I hear people like, "Oh, I can't know the science. I'm not a scientist." Hell yeah, you can learn the science. It's not a massive secret. If you're interested in science, you can go directly; you don't have to listen to me. You go on something like Google Scholar, and you go and say— if you're interested in depression and sunshine, you go to Google Scholar, you type in "depression sunshine review paper" or "depression sunshine meta-analysis." Meta-analysis is basically a quantitative analysis of papers. You go in there, and you find a meta-analysis that looks pretty recent, and you see how many people have cited it. It'll say how many people cited, meaning they wrote a paper and referred back to that meta- analysis. You go, "Oh, there's a meta-analysis here that's been cited a hundred times." That's where you start, and you read that.
1.112: It's not that hard to get into the literature. The thing you're not going to be able to do if you're not a professional is you don't know when people are lying, and you don't know how people are shading the truth because there's a lot of stuff in science where people are telling the story one way and if you don't know the technical stuff, it's hard to see through it. But beyond that stuff, reading the science, it's totally out there, a nd I'm saying, "Go for it. Just start reading papers." And you can find them. If you can't find them, you could email me, "Hey, can I have a copy of your paper?" And I might even send it to you because no one asks me for my papers. Most academics go, "Oh, my God, somebody cares. Everyone hates me. This person, though, this person in Guam loves my work," and they're very happy to share it.
1.113: So, I would just finish up by saying I encourage you. Whatever you're interested in, whatever you learn here, if you want to go for it, just go and read the original research yourself. Read the books. You don't have to listen to other people talking about it because people who spend their life talking about other people's research are generally not people you want to listen to. People you're going to listen to are doing it themselves. 2. Mental Models and Sense-Making At a glance Human beings turn incomplete information into workable mental models. This lecture examines perception, attention, memory, heuristics, schemas, attribution, bias, prediction, and social sense-making, showing how useful shortcuts can also distort judgment. It emphasizes that cognition is embodied, selective, shaped by context, and influenced by other people.
2.1: Welcome back. What I wanted to talk about in this session was the big question of the psychology of human behavior, which is how we make sense of the world. So, how we take information in and turn it into something sensible, and how we operate with that.
2.2: So, it's easy to think that we are humans, that we see the world, and we work like a recording device. I walk into this room; I have stuff come in through my senses: my eyes, my ears, my touch, my smell. We have lots of senses. And then, I record it in my mind, in my memory, and I could play it back later. But I'm seeing pretty much what the world is. That's not how it works, unfortunately. It would be cool if you could record everything and call it back at will, and maybe some of the new AI cameras you're going to wear are going to do that, but that's not how we're built. That's how our computer is built.
2.3: What we do is we run across the thing in itself, the world out there. And the world out there is really complicated, and there's so much going on, and it's very hard to make sense of it. So, we take that world in through our senses. We reduce it down to a model, like a small diorama of the world that's related to what we need to do, it's related to our motivations, it's something we've built over time, and we operate from that model.
2.4: So, what we're not doing is seeing everything. I can't see ultraviolet light. I can't hear things my dog hears. And even the stuff I see, I'm often not paying attention to because if I paid attention to everything around me, I would lose my mind. If I looked at what everyone in this audience is wearing and tried to figure out what it was, I couldn't talk. So, you got to do a lot of reduction. And so, what we have is the gap between the thing in itself and this little model of the mind. In psychology, we call this sensation and perception.
2.5: So, this sensation is what we take into our sensory apparatus, our eyes or ears, or whatever; it goes through our neural system. There's a lot of great science on this. And our perception is what we see after we've reintegrated this into our mind. And what we see is different than what's out there. So, that break in the world is really important to understand, that the world is really small. And like I said, most of the time we don't notice, but you can see how the mind is in the process of constructing a model with different things.
2.6: So, one of the things you notice in the human condition is pareidolia. I always pronounced that wrong, and I've even looked it up. I think maybe there is no right way. Pareidolia— essentially what we do if we take ambiguous objects, you look at clouds, you look at the front of a car, you look at normal things, we tend to put those into things like faces or animals or other things that are meaningful. We turn ambiguous stuff into something we understand.

2.21: So, given these constraints on our working model, the self, and our sense-making, what we've developed as humans is what's called a dual process or two-system model of the mind. 2.43: So, a script is a model of sequential action for an event. So, imagine I go to a restaurant tonight, a restaurant I had never been to. 2.60: And you also recall, I mentioned that our belief about the world, our model of the world, needs to be consistent. For us to feel good, we have to have consistency. It leads to what they call dissonance, which is a feeling of psychological discomfort coupled with a motivation to get out of that because we're not built to feel dissonance. Trying to think how far back to take this. So, Festinger got interested in this process.

So, you hear the term 'persona,' persona is the word for mask, and so the term 'personality' is basically our modern term for the person's mask; the character they wear through life.
5.3: Often when we talk about personality models, we're talking about more quantitative models. These are things that we develop with pretty intense statistics. We develop pretty good tests or assessments for personality traits. So, we're measuring personality that way.
5.4: One way to think about personality traits are a consistent pattern of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors across time and situation. So, when we think about something like a personality trait, it's a way I act across time. So, I'm like this two years ago, I'm like this now. I'll probably be the same way tomorrow. And across situations, I'll probably act this way here, but probably in other situations as well. So, it's a consistency about behavior, but it's also about what makes me different than other people. So, it's a consistency that's different. We call this individual differences. People are different.
5.5: In my case, I'm pretty energized. There's some reason: I'm extroverted, I'm neurotic, and you bring those two powerful forces together and put me on the stage, and I start wiggling like a little gopher. That's my extraversion. I'm extroverted here. When I talk to the cab driver on the way home, I'm going to be chatting about the meaning of life. When I go to get dinner tonight, I'll be chatting with everybody. Everyone's going to hate me by the end of the night. That's just how I am. I'll go to the funeral at the end of the world, the great apocalypse funeral, and I'm going to be chatting with the demons, "Hey, guys, how you doing? I dig those spears." My nature. That's a personality trait.
5.6: Self is a little different. 'Self' is a word that's more—it comes out of old English, Indo- European. It basically means 'separate' or 'one's own.' So, the self is about what's mine. There's a weird thing that happens in science. Things that come from English or Germanic roots sound dumb, and things that come from Latin or Greek roots sound smart and sophisticated. So, when you say, "I'm interested in the personality," they go, "That sounds sophisticated." You say, "I'm a self researcher," they go, "That sounds kind of dumb."
5.7: That's a little trick you can—I learned that from reading Huxley, actually, but it's a little trick, like my watch versus my chronometer; the chronometer sounds a little sexier than a watch. So, these are kind of similar things, but they're a little different.
5.8: When we think about the self in psychology, it's a little more about our narrative, it's a little bit more about our story, how we see our self. It's a little bit more about how we evaluate our self, our self-esteem, our self-conception. So, it's a little richer concept, it's a little more, I don't know; it's got a little more blood and guts to it. But essentially, these are the same things. These are what makes you a person who's different than other people and how you're wired.
5.9: So, I thought what I would do today is—I want to talk about classic quantitative personality models, and I'm going to focus on what's called the Big Five or five-factor model, or OCEAN, which you might be familiar with. It's our most popular, most useful model, I think. And then, I'm going to talk about some approaches to the self, and I'm going to base it on William James's classic work on the self in his chapter in the Principles of Psychology, the basic: how the self works, here are the parts, think about it.
5.10: In terms of the research on personality traits, it's a really interesting historical effort. So, researchers, maybe 120 years ago, back in the UK, started thinking, "Hey, we want to understand personality. We understand how people's personality can be modeled and how it changes over time and across generations," and so they said, "Well, how do we measure personality?"
5.11: Well, there's an idea, and I think it was Sir Francis Galton who came up with this; I could be wrong; he came up with this idea that we now call the lexical hypothesis, 'lexical' meaning 'word' or 'lexicon.' The idea is that if there's a personality trait that matters to describe somebody, like if this is useful for describing people in the world, our language, and indeed every language, will come up with a single word for that thing.
5.12: So, if it's really useful to describe something like, "Hey, that person's really smart," I'm going to come up with a word that's 'smart.' I'm not going to say, "You know, that person's one of those people that's really good at, like, you give them puzzles, and they figure it out fast, and they seem to be a little quick to figure things out. I don't know what. There must be a word for that." We don't say that. We go, "They're smart; they're clever." So, we come up with words.
5.13: Every once in a while, we don't have a word in English that we need, and we go steal it from somebody else. And all languages do this. So, we might say, like, a great psychological word that we use is Schadenfreude. This isn't really a trait, but it's a word we took from German, meaning 'I take pleasure in other people's suffering.' We don't have a good English word for that, so we steal a German word.
5.14: So, occasionally, we do that, but generally, what happens is we build these single words to describe personality traits, and these are trait adjectives. How do you describe somebody? So, psychologists started looking at these trait words. It turns out there's a whole lot of them, in English in particular, because we're a combination language from German and Latin, where we have a lot of words, a lot of interesting words, but all languages have lots of traits. We have something like 4,500 traits. I've seen more; I've seen less, depending, but that's a lot of traits.
5.15: What do you do with 4,500 traits? Well, you can't make a personality model with 4,500 variables. "Hey, Keith, we're going to bring you in the lab. We're going to nail down your personality on these 4,500 different dimensions, and then we're going to build a map." Like, dude, that's not going to do me any good. That's a too complicated map. Remember? As a psychologist, I'm trying to make a simple, dumb map that I can use for a lot of things. Not a super complicated map. That's called a picture.
5.16: So, what psychologists started doing was saying, "Well, maybe we can group these traits into smaller groups." There's different ways you do that mathematically. You can do something like a factor analysis, which is a way of looking at how things correlate and putting them into buckets. You can look at them with coders and say, "Yeah, these sound the same." And so what they did was started taking all these words and putting them into buckets.
5.17: So, imagine I've got 45,000 trait words up here; there's a million words. There's— whenever I do this, I always come up with weird words: conniving and kleptomaniac. That's—I don't know if that's a word. Conniving, and curious, and cadaverous, and I don't know, dizzy, and silly, and kind, and cooperative, and compassionate, and extroverted. All these different terms. So, there's thousands of those.
5.18: But imagine you have five big buckets in front of us, or maybe ten buckets. It doesn't matter. And you start putting words in buckets that are similar. So, like, "Oh, kind, I'll put in that bucket. How about friendly? Well, that sounds like it's the same bucket. How about compassionate? Yeah, it's pretty much the same. How about nice? Well, that's in that bucket. How about angry? That doesn't sound the same, but it's kind of the same. I don't know." So, angry maybe goes in that bucket, and maybe it goes in the neuroticism bucket. I don't know.
5.19: So, what happens is you start building these buckets. When you do that, you end up with five buckets. Five big buckets that do a pretty good job. It isn't magic. It's not like God made five buckets for personality traits, and thank God I found them. They're in the Geneva Bible. You have to read it in the original old Dutch or something. It's not like that; we make these things up. But five works pretty well. Six works okay. You can also do three or two or one. They all work, but five tends to be what they are.
5.20: And those five buckets that we put traits into are called "The Big Five," sometimes "The Five Factor Model." People have come at it with personality tests and come at it different ways and get the same five. Often, we call this model OCEAN for the simple reason that the names of each of the five buckets, the first letter spell 'ocean' or 'canoe,' and no one wants to be on the canoe model because that sounds lame, but the ocean model sounds cool. So, think about these traits as OCEAN.
5.21: And what do they spell? Well, 'O' is for 'openness to experience.' I'll go into these in detail in a minute, but to give you an overview. 'O' is for 'openness to experience.' That's an interest in art, esthetics, creativity, curiosity. It's a trait you see with artists, designers, etcetera.
5.22: The 'C' is for 'conscientiousness.' This is a trait that has to do with organization, discipline, dutifulness, industriousness, and hard work. Conscientiousness is the trait of the workplace, predicts a lot of high level performance at work.
5.23: The 'E' is for 'extraversion.' Extraversion is what most of you think, which is sociability, but extraversion also has a big dose of assertiveness. It's this drive and energy. So, you see a lot of extraversion in leadership. So, I'll meet people like, "Yeah, I run a Fortune 500 company, and I do this and do that, but I'm not an extrovert." I think, "Dude, you're an extrovert. You're just not very social." "Oh, that's true. I like to be out there. I like to make stuff happen." So, these are big traits, meaning they're big buckets. There's a lot going on. There's a lot of complexity even within them.
5.24: The 'A' is for 'agreeableness.' Agreeableness means, essentially, it has to be nice, kind, cooperative, and polite. So, it has to do with getting along, like swimming with a school of fish. It also has to do with deep compassion, so you can be a nice person who's deeply caring, a nice person who's really cooperative.
5.25: And then, the 'N' is for neuroticism. Neuroticism is basically a combination of fearfulness, maybe anxiety, depression, and also vulnerability. You get overwhelmed easily. So, I get overwhelmed by events. I feel like I can't get up and fight the battle more. I'm taken over. So, it's the sense of being overwhelmed.
5.26: When you think about those traits, we often say openness instead of openness to experience; it's shorter. But openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism, that's the big five. These generally sound positive. They all generally sound positive. So, openness sounds positive. Conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness. But neuroticism sounds a little negative, right? Does that sound right? Yeah. And that's what you see that makes it a little confusing. So, sometimes people will flip neuroticism and call it emotional stability, so they're all a little positive.
5.27: But here's the thing about these traits, a few things. This is like the basic rules of personality traits. It applies to The Big Five, but really, any trait we study. First of all, these things are on a continuum or continua, not your continuums. They're not types. So, if you see personality tests that put you into a type, like you're an extrovert and you're an introvert, those don't do well because nature doesn't really make types. What nature makes are continua. They make distributions of people.
5.28: Most of us, really, about two-thirds of us are going to be right around the middle point of any one of these traits. Trait openness: most of us are around the middle. Some of us are going to be pretty open. That might be how we see ourselves. Some of us might be so open —that is what we call our cardinal trait. This is our primary trait. I'm an open guy. Some of us are going to be much more conventionally minded: "Dude, I don't do that stuff. I just chill. It sounds a little weird to me, man." Some people are like that. Most of us are in the middle. That's the nature of traits.
5.29: The other thing to remember is that both extremes can be good or bad, depending on context. There's a little bit of a bias in our culture where people, like I said, want to be more extroverted, typically. But if I ask a class of 300 people, how many of you want to be more extroverted? I'll get a bunch of people say, "I'd like to be more extroverted," and I'll say, "How many of you want to be less extroverted and more introverted?" And I'll get a few people.
5.30: Sometimes, I'm one of those people that go, "I'm a little too extroverted. It gets me into trouble." I have trouble talking to people sometimes because they go, "I have an idea," a nd I talk for 10 minutes about their idea because I'm a bad listener. Sometimes, I do crazy stuff; I say crazy stuff. My extraversion gets me in trouble.
5.31: So, you can have trouble on either side, even though there's a little bit of a bias. Okay, so when we talk about the clinical stuff in a few classes from now, you're gonna see clinical bias in one way, but really, you can have problems on both sides, and a lot of it depends on social context.
5.32: If you're in a real threatening environment, being neurotic is awesome because you're out there, "I'm looking for threats," and people that aren't neurotic are going to get eaten. But when it's a very safe environment, people who are neurotic aren't going to do as well because they're going to be nervous all the time, and people who are more risk-taking will do well. So, a lot of this depends on context.
5.33: These traits are all very heritable. This was a question someone asked last time about happiness, and it applies to most personality traits. When we look at the behavioral genetics, which means we're looking at the family history of traits, not the genes themselves, we find about 40%, give or take, is inherited through our family structure.
5.34: So, the way I'm wired looks like certain people in my family. I look at my kids and I go, "Well, you got some of me and some of your mom, and some of your uncle Bill. You got little pieces of each of us, and that's how you're wired up to start; not much you can do about it when you start." You can do something about it once you get older and you can start to modify your personality.
5.35: But it's very much when I talk to people about personalities, we're wired differently. People are just different. People are different, and those differences matter. Those differences make a difference. People are different, and those differences make a difference. People have very different approaches to things.
5.36: So, even though personality is heritable, it can be changeable. There's lots of interesting work now on personality change. What we're seeing—and I'll talk about this more with the clinical work—but what you see is when people change their personality, it's about what we'd say a third of a standard deviation. I don't know what that means. How do I translate a third of a standard deviation? It's like five IQ points out of 100; that's about a third of a standard deviation. Maybe in height, it would be like I gained an inch or two. So, no one's making me tall, but if I got an inch or two, at least I'd have some self-esteem. So, that's what it is. It moves people a little bit.
5.37: You typically don't see people going from, "Yeah, I was really this way to totally this way." Usually, the change is a little bit more on a continuum. Sometimes, you get that real radical quantum change, but typically, it's a more moderate change. But change is certainly possible. There's a lot of research on this now. And people think, "Yeah, this stuff's set in stone." Freud used to say that personality stopped at age six. And I think James said it was cast in plaster at 30. It's not true; personality changes your whole life.
5.38: Personality is reflected everywhere. It leaves traces. Your personality leaves traces in everything you do. So, I can guess your personality from your outfits. I can guess your personality from your appearance. I can guess your personality by looking at your office. I can look at your bedroom deck. And this is all from research. I can look at your bedroom. I can look at your car. I can look at everything. I can look at your Facebook page or your Instagram, and I can detect personality in everything.
5.39: It leaves what they call personality traces. It's like, I imagine you're walking around with pixie dust, leaving your personality everywhere. 5.42: All these things could be measured quantitatively very easy. We have what's called self- report measures, which are essentially: here's a list of questions, answer these questions, and we can tell your personality. We can measure your Big Five personality.

5.52: Trait agreeableness is another one of these interesting traits. The three facets of that— these are from the Big Five inventory, too—are compassion, respectfulness, and trust. 5.53: Respectfulness is all different. Respectfulness isn't so much about caring. It's about being a good member of a community. I respect the rules of the community, I respect other people, I'm a good citizen. So, it's more about cooperation and getting along.
5.54: And finally, there's this piece of trust. I trust people when I'm agreeable. 5.73: And so, this quality of consciousness, this 'I,' this experience of being alive, this observer of consciousness, is very hard to study, and it's maybe the core of who we are. 5.74: So, if I want to say, "Show me your self-concept." You'd go, "Well, I'm a psychologist, and I like fast cars and good steak." That was a Bill Murray reference from the ' 70s no one would get. 5.77: And James talked about several different parts of the self-concept. I'm going to talk about four of them. 5.78: When we have a self-concept, we have an evaluation of that or an attitude about that. "Hey, Keith. Do you like Keith, or do you not like Keith?" 5.79: Typically, people don't hate themselves. If you really hate yourself, that becomes more clinical pathology, usually, because you have a self. Usually, I really like it or I kind of like it. Most people's self-esteem is pretty high. So, that's how we think about self-esteem, as evaluation.
5.80: William James had this interesting model. He said that self-esteem was your aspirations divided by your pretensions. Basically, what you aspire to in life versus what you actually accomplish, what you see yourself accomplishing. If you aspire to be president of the United States and you can't even make it to mayor in your town, your self-esteem is going to be low. If you aspire to be—if you aspire to run for County Dog Catcher and you become the mayor, you're going to be the happiest guy on earth. So, a lot of this has to do in James's world with how we expect things.
5.81: James has a story. He ran into a Civil War soldier from the South who lost everything. He said he was rolling in the dirt he was so happy. Why was he so happy? So, the idea with James is that self-esteem is something that depends on what we want and how well we're getting there.
5.82: Modern research on self-esteem focuses a little differently. Often, we think of self-esteem as a core, positive self-view. It's a positive self-knowledge. Like, I feel love deep inside that comes from early attachment. So, people talk about this early self-esteem we get from early experiences of love. That's almost like a resource, meaning if times get hard, I look inward and feel this love.
5.83: Another way people have talked about self-esteem now is more of a meter of how you're doing. So, people say, "Ah, self-esteem is a sociometer," meaning it tells you if you're belonging. If you're connected with people, your self-esteem will be high. If your self- esteem is low, maybe you're not connected with people.
5.84: Other researchers argue maybe it's a hierarchy meter. I'm not even saying that r ight. It shows you where you are in the hierarchy. So, if your status is good, you feel self- esteem. If your status drops, your self-esteem goes down, like a gage on a car. So, self-esteem does a lot of things. It can be a resource. It can be a signal telling us how well we can do, how well we're doing. It can be something we really think about and evaluate. Self-esteem is generally pretty high. Like I said, most college students have pretty high self-esteem. We measure something called the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Inventory. I gave you a couple of questions off that.
5.85: And in terms of the benefits of self-esteem, despite the self-esteem movement in California in the '70 and '80 and this massive interest in self-esteem and giving kids self-esteem, it doesn't seem to be super beneficial. Self-esteem is really good for fighting depression. So, if you look at a lot of the research, people with high self-esteem—that seems to be a buffer against depression. So, that's really important. Self-esteem seems to be good for starting things. So, people with self-esteem are a little more willing to initiate action, but other than that, it's not some magic thing.
5.86: You get lots of very successful people who hate themselves, and they talk to me, "Dude, I hate myself." I'm like, "Welcome to the club. It's okay. We all do," and everyone hugs. It does seem to be something I'd want my kids to have. It does seem to be a pretty good buffer for things. So, esteem is evaluation.

5.90: So, what we're doing is we buy stuff to fill out our self-concept, and we do it with our clothes, we do it with stuff. And you get a lot of neat phenomena because of this. 5.92: Country music songs: what do you do? Your boyfriend cheats on you, the first thing to do? You go burn their car. 5.93: So, this material self is something we really focus on. We do it with our looks. A lot of life is what we call identity negotiation. This is no sociological idea, but I will dress in a certain way so people treat me a certain way, and if they don't, it's going to be a little weird. So, if I wear—I'm wearing this casual outfit. That means I'm approachable. You can talk to me. If I were wearing a suit and it was a little more grim, people would go, I'm a little less approachable. 5.94: When I'm on a college campus, everybody's dressed according to their social status. So, if I see somebody with their Grateful Dead outfit and I'm like, "Hey, what sorority you're in?" 5.96: The next part of the self James talked about was the social self. What James said was, "Properly speaking, a man has as many social selves as there are individuals who recognize him and carry an image of him in their minds." So, what James was saying is that you feel like you have a single self, and you do, but that self changes depending on the groups you're with.
5.97: His example was, imagine you're a young boy. You're hanging out with your friends, acting like pirates. And you're running around going, "We're going to go plunder." That's what you're thinking. You're going to do damage and plunder, and then you go home to mom. You're a very different person with mom. You're not talking about plundering. You go to church, you're sitting up nicely, you're dressed up. You're not plundering.
5.98: So, you have these different roles, and you act differently in different roles. And you see this. You'd be an adult, and you go home for Christmas, and you go, "God, I felt like a kid. It was all creepy. I was just saying—I was yelling at my mom like I was 14. What happened to me? I don't even like this person." Well, you came into another social self. You activated a social self based on the context, and you acted differently because of that. So that's just how social selves work.
5.99: Some people are more isolated. Their social selves are more discreet. There's an old Seinfeld episode with George again, where he had a girlfriend, but he never would have his girlfriend meet his friend Jerry because he was like, "Well, there's the girlfriend George and the friend George, and they're totally different. If they met, it would be a nuclear explosion." That's a joke because it's showing a neurotic aspect of having selves that are totally different. But it's a joke, and it's a good joke because it's kind of true.
5.100: You have a girlfriend, Keith, and then a cool guy, Keith. And the girlfriend, Keith, is all nice and soft, and the cool guy, Keith, is a tough guy. And then, your cool guys see you with your girlfriend, and then they make fun of you. So, you're like, "I'll just keep those two apart." That's how it works.
5.101: Another really interesting thing with the social self is what's called the Looking Glass Self. And this is an old idea from sociology, Charles Horton Cooley. A looking glass is an old- fashioned term for a mirror, like Alice in Wonderland through the looking glass. So, the idea of the looking glass self was the mirror self.
5.102: So, imagine this. I walk into a group of people, "Hey." And everyone just goes like this. What am I going to think about myself? "Oh, my God, I'm a horrible person. What did I do wrong? Everyone's doing this." I walk into another group, and everyone's like, "Yes." Doing this, high five, and I'm like, "I feel so good about myself. This is awesome. You guys are cool. I was happy to come to them. These guys were nice. I feel good." We learn about ourselves by watching the reactions in other people.
5.103: Other people are like a mirror for us, and we pick up these cues very subtly and very quickly. We learn them from our parents. We learn them from our young children. But even as adults, we pick up the cues in the environment. And so, we're constantly being shaped. Our self-concept is constantly being shaped by the social reactions we see around us, and it's happening all the time. It's a constant reinforcement stream we're not really aware of.
5.104: The general rule in life is if you don't like yourself, surround yourself with people who like you because my guess is you probably got some people sucking the energy out of you, like vampires, to fill the hole in their soul. And so, our self-concept is very socially dependent. It's not a bad thing. Just be smart about who you hang out with.
5.105: Finally, James talked about what's called the spiritual self. And the spiritual self is a person's "inner or subjective being and psychic faculties or dispositions." So, what James meant about the spiritual self is that this is where consciousness is. This is where the 'I' is. Again, I can't explain what the 'I' is, but that's where it is. It's your moral center. It's your sense of character, righteousness, goodness.
5.106: A hundred years ago, that's what people cared about. Now, we care about personality traits because it's very individualized, kind of pop society. A hundred years ago, it was much more about morals, personal worth, but same idea. It's where cognitive abilities are. Cognitive faculty, intelligence, cleverness, creativity, all those would be in the spiritual self, and all the classic personality traits would be in there. 5.107: I mentioned this to one of the questions here, but the term spiritual self, you'll notice in a lot of textbooks it got swapped out with psychological self because people can't handle spiritual. 5.108: And then, the final thing I wanted to talk about, which, I think, is interesting to really wrap up the self stuff before the narratives, is the true self. 5.131: The big story that we talk about is the hero's journey, and this is one you're probably familiar with. The hero's journey is the cycle of the individual starting as a person, being called to an adventure either by luck or by being blown off course. Darth Vader comes and kills his family, and he's got to go do something. Or he gets an owl come in and starts throwing him letters, and then Hagrid grabs him on a bike and says, "Time for going to magic world." Whatever it is.
5.132: You're called to an adventure. You get some allies, you have a bunch of conflicts, you go through some real deep conflicts, you have a battle at the end. 5.133: So, the classic hero's journey is the journey to find yourself. It's Odysseus: you go to war, you get blown off course, you go through all these different tests, and you become a hero by going through tests, and then you return. 5.134: So, Hercules, the first hero, named after Hera, the goddess who sent him on these journeys, Hercules goes through his twelve tests: g oes, kills a lion, cleans a bunch of stalls, has to get a fawn, just all these different challenges that line up with the constellations. 5.135: This idea of the hero's journey goes back to a psychoanalyst named Otto Ronk, who talked about it in development. But then, a gentleman named Joseph Campbell, who was a professor at Sarah Lawrence, a mythologist, he studied Freudian models and a lot of Carl Jung's work, and then he studied a lot of the anthropological models, and what he developed was something called—he wrote a book called The Hero with a Thousand Faces.
5.136: I don't know if you're familiar with this. I think Jimmy Buffett has a song about this, too.
