Every movie you watch, the person writing the movie is reading Joseph Campbell and writing the hero's journey in on it. So, they're all on this archetype.
5.137: And so, there's some narrative to life that we follow, and this idea of the hero's journey, which is, I start someplace, I get called to an adventure, I face tests, I succeed in those tests, and I come back home with some knowledge for other people. That cycle seems to be one of the most important stories we tell ourselves. We love that story. We tell it all the time. We like to look at our own life as a hero's journey.
5.138: I guess to wrap up here, in terms of the self, it's very easy to figure out who we are by breaking it down, to figure out how our traits are built, to figure out how our self-system's built, but the movement in life, to be an integrated person, so you feel like I'm one person doing one journey, I'm not just a bunch of parts in a big machine, you're telling yourself a story, and you're taking risks, and you're facing challenges. Thanks. 7. Mental Health At a glance Clinical psychology studies psychological distress, diagnosis, and treatment. The lecture reviews major forms of mental illness, competing biological and psychosocial explanations, the limits of diagnostic categories, medication, psychotherapy, stigma, resilience, and the practical challenge of deciding when and how to seek help.
7.1: What I want to talk to you about today is clinical psychology, psychopathology, mental illness. This is a huge field of psychology.
7.2: Most people, when they think about psychology, want to go into psychology, want to be a clinician or a clinical psychologist. And I should say it's a little different deal. So, I have a clinical PhD, but I'm not a licensed clinical psychologist. 7.3: Mental illness and the interest in mental illness didn't just start with psychology. So, we talk about psychology starting in maybe the middle of the 1800s, but people were dealing with mental illness before then. So, you can read old case reports in different literatures around the world, but in the European system. For example, my work on narcissism, the first case reports I've seen were from the 1700s, where they had a narcissistic mania reported in France.
7.4: And so, you have lots of disorders people were talking about. They didn't quite know what to do with them. So, a lot of times people would have what looks like a psychiatric disorder, but they treat it in a medical way. 7.5: So, this isn't brand new stuff. What's happened with modern psychology and psychiatry is we've got all these disorders; we're trying to make sense of them. How do we organize these disorders into something useful? And then, how do we treat these disorders?
7.6: Clinical psychology, or abnormal psychology, you might want to call it, or the psychology of mental disorders, has also often involved psychologists, but also involves psychiatrists. So psychiatrists are medical doctors or MDs, and they have a medical degree, but then they go into additional training in psychiatry. So, it's very similar, but they tend to be a little more focused on both in psychiatry: a little more focused on using drug therapies or other medical interventions, and also a little more focused on psychoanalysis, which is strange, but a lot of the real Freudian stuff still happens in medical schools and psychiatric programs. 7.7: So, what I thought I would do is I'm going to talk about what a mental illness is or what psychopathology is. Psychopathology is just a fancy word for pathology, the breaking down of the psyche. I got soul problems. You got soul problems. That's what's going on. You got psychopathology. We call it mental illness.
7.8: So, what I thought I would do is talk a little bit about what a mental illness is, how we can think about what these are. 7.9: There are so many disorders out there. There's so many little trichotillomania, pulling your hair out to help you deal with anxiety. There's just thousands of little disorders. You could be a specialist in mood disorders, maybe a specialist in one personality disorder after PhD. So, it's pretty broad stuff.
7.10: So, the first question is, what is psychopathology? And according to the American Psychiatric Association—so, when we have our big book of mental disorders, it's called the DSM, the Diagnostics and Statistics Manual. I get that wrong all the time. They have different versions of that. We're up to five now. And that's put together by the American Psychiatric Association. So, it's the physicians; there's usually some clinical psychologists in the mix working on it, but it's done by the psychiatrists, not the American Psychological Association, which gets confusing.
7.11: So, these descriptions of disorders that I'm going to give you and talk about are done for clinical diagnosis. If you're a physician, you can only treat somebody who's sick. 7.12: What is a disorder? Well, the first thing you get is a clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotion, or behavior. What does that mean? Well, the 'clinically significant,' that's where a trained clinician, psychiatrist, psychologist, says, "This disorder is messing you up enough that we should treat you." This isn't just every day you're a little sad. This is a clinically significant amount of sadness that deserves treatment. So, they have to find a line there, what's significant and what's not. That's an art. They get trained, but there 's no AI that does it or something or a chart; you make that decision as a physician.
7.13: And then, in terms of where you see these disturbances, the first is cognition. Cognition is our fancy word for thoughts. You have issues with your thoughts. Maybe your thoughts are delusional. Maybe you have a belief about the world that doesn't accurately capture the world. Maybe your thoughts are a little paranoid. Maybe you feel that there's forces in the world that are out to get you when they're not. Maybe your thoughts are shaded towards the negative. Maybe you think no matter what you do, nothing will work out, nothing will ever go your way, even though you seem to be like somebody who it should go your way. Maybe your thoughts race too fast. They move so quickly that you can't really catch up with them. Maybe that's a little bit of mania, a little hypomania, a low level of mania. So, your thoughts are a little out of control. So, you can have a lot of things go on with your thoughts in different ways.
7.14: And then, there's emotional issues you can have. What are emotional problems? Well, maybe you feel a little blue or sad. So, maybe there's some sad emotion and that's bringing you down. Maybe you have more fearful emotion. Maybe you're anxious all the time. Maybe you see threats in the environment. Maybe you're wired to see lots of threats in the environment, maybe so many threats you can't function well. So, it could be that emotional issue.

7.16: Or you can have behavioral issues. So, this is the third. So, maybe you have problems gambling. Maybe you're drinking or smoking too much weed or whatever it is. You're doing something that's messing up your life.
7.17: So, all those different things can be problems, and they can be problems in different ways. There 's lots of ways you're behavior can be a problem, lots of ways your emotion, lots of ways your cognition. So, that's the first thing.
7.18: The second thing to be a disorder is it has to be based on some underlying psychology, biology or development, meaning that for something to be a clinical disorder, like depression, you say, "Well, there's something going on psychologically." Maybe it was a series of loss. Maybe it was something to do in childhood that you can't really resolve. Maybe it's something biological. Maybe it's the level of serotonin in your system is unstable, and that's leading to the depression. Or maybe it's a developmental disorder. So maybe it 's something that happened in your developmental trajectory, your brain got filled with fluid, you had some constraint, and that led to the problem. So usually, for a mental disorder, psychopathology, there's some grounding in psychobiology or development.
7.19: It wouldn't be—I'm trying to think of an example. It's weird. If you have, like Phineas Gage, you have a steel rod go through your head and you can't remember things, in some ways, that's a psychology problem, but really, it's you got a metal rod through your head problem, and you get the metal rod out, and then you maybe heal up the psychology. I don't know if that's psychopathology or if that's just the side effects of a stroke. Those are where it gets tenuous.
7.20: Mental disorders usually feel bad, meaning they're associated with what we call distress, and I've said this before several times, in love and work. This is going back to Freud. So if you have a mental disorder, usually it's messing up your relationships, your marriage, your friendships, your romantic life, how you get along with your parents, or it's messing up your ability to work. You can't do as well in work because you got something going on.
7.21: There are a few exceptions of mental disorders that don't seem to be impairing, at least at first, but they hurt everybody else. So, it's harder to see, for example, in my own work with narcissism, with extreme narcissism, sometimes you get people that are like, "Yeah, I feel pretty good. I'm working pretty well. My marriage is good." And you go talk to their family like, "No, it's not good at all. It's a nightmare." 7.22: Sometimes, substance abuse will do this. "Yeah, I'm using amphetamines to help me perform better at work," or "I'm micro-dosing something at work, and it's awesome." 7.23: When you're depressed, you're like, "I don't feel good." Anxiety doesn't feel good. It might be useful to be anxious sometimes. I'm about to walk on stage back here. 7.24: A couple of other things about disorders. First, it can't be a culturally normative behavior. So, you don't want to do something that's culturally normative and diagnose it as a disorder. There's a long history of doing this in different countries, and you try to avoid it. So, there's a couple of big examples of this that you run into.
7.25: The first is grief or bereavement. You lose your spouse, you lose your loved one, p eople will go into depression, and that's pretty normal. If I met somebody, "I lost my husband," and they're depressed, I'm like, "Well, God, I'm really sorry." You don 't go, "Snap out of it." It's, "I feel for you. I hope you get out of this. 7.26: But if somebody is depressed, it's been a year or two, and they're still—they can't get out of bed, then you start going, "Well, maybe this has turned from a normal cultural bereavement into something else. 7.27: The other thing you sometimes get are odd religious practices or beliefs. 7.28: And the final thing is a mental disorder isn't supposed to be about a conflict between an individual in a society. You're a mentally ill criminal." It's still a criminal, but there's a mental illness along with that.
7.29: So, it can be complicated, but generally, we don't put criminality as mental illness, except for in those cases where you have forensics experts in there, and you're saying, "Is this person mentally fit to stand trial?" which is pretty rare.
7.30: You also don't see it with something like terrorism or political warfare. Somebody is like, "I'm going to kill people because I believe in my God, or I believe in my political place. 7.31: So again, this is a complicated thing to think about what mental illness is. But, generally, you have some major disturbance in thoughts, feelings, behaviors. It leads to problems. It can be diagnosed. It's not easily put into some other category. That would be a mental illness.
7.32: There are, like I said, there are a huge number of these disorders that you run into all the time. And so, you'll go—and they're outlined in the DSM— but when you go visit a psychologist or psychiatrist, you go in there, typically, what's not happening is they're not doing a super diagnosis on you. If I go walk into a psychologist right now down the street, and he says, "Dude, how do you feel?" "Man, I'm anxious. I'm sad. I have trouble sleeping sometimes." They go, "Well, you sound like you got some anxiety. You want to talk about it? Here's a pill." Boom. They give you a benzo, or they give you an SSRI.
7.33: There's typically not a really deep diagnosis done. You do it in clinical settings. We do it in clinical research sometimes. Sometimes, you can hire somebody to do a clinical diagnosis, maybe for a learning disorder or something. There are ways to do it, but it's typically—we don't do a lot of heavy diagnosis. You 'll probably notice that if you ever go in a mental health setting, it's not like, "Hey, we got to spend the first week and run you through $5,000 of diagnostic protocol." We don't do a lot of diagnosis. We just put people into buckets.
7.34: The reason we do that is because a lot of these disorders are overlapping, and they have similar treatments. So, if I have someone come in and they're a little anxious or a little depressed, I go, "They're probably going to respond to a little cognitive therapy, a little support, maybe some SSRI." I don't need to get real into the weeds about what's going on. "We'll see if this works. If it doesn't work, then I'll get into the weeds." So, it's often cheaper just to treat people for what's common and then go back.
7.35: What's happened is we've developed a couple of different ways of making sense of the disorders and organizing them. So, I 'd say the old way, but it's still what people are doing, you'll divide disorders into two major what they call axes. So, you'd say, "Hey, these are the disorders that are like diseases, the Axis I disorders." They feel like a disease. You were healthy, and then you got this disease, and now I'm going to treat it like a physician.
7.36: So, you're a happy-go-lucky person, you end up feeling some depression, or you end up feeling anxiety, or you end up, God forbid, at your young age, you end up with a schizophrenic break. 7.37: The other type of disorders back in the day—the two main types, there's others—is Axis II disorders, and those are personality disorders. So, Axis I disorders are these psychological diseases, and the Axis II disorders are called personality disorders. They used to be called character disorders, disorders of character.
7.38: So, what a personality disorder is, it's an extreme and inflexible configuration of personality that leads to clinically significant impairment. The idea, though, with a personality disorder is that it's part of you; you've had something your whole life.
